findings.message: `self.skipWaiting()` is called unconditionally in the `install` handler, so the service worker never enters a 'waiting' state. This means every SW update immediately takes over all open tabs, triggering the `controllerchange` → `window.location.reload()` path in dashboard.js without any user coordination — the page reloads abruptly mid-session regardless of what the user is doing. The intent of the SKIP_WAITING message system (letting the page decide when to hand off) is completely bypassed by this line.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `self.skipWaiting()` is unconditionally called in the install handler (line 17, pre-existing). This means the SW never enters a waiting state. The PR adds a `controllerchange` listener that calls `window.location.reload()` — combined with the unconditional skipWaiting, this causes immediate mid-session page reloads on every SW update without the user coordination the SKIP_WAITING message system was designed to provide.
findings.severity_justification: Causes unexpected page reloads mid-session on every SW deployment, potentially disrupting users. Not data-loss level but a real UX regression that contradicts the PR's stated intent of controlled update handoff.
findings.category_justification: The logic is self-contradictory: the SW never waits (skipWaiting in install), so the SKIP_WAITING message coordination the client-side code relies on can never work as intended.

findings.message: The `message` event handler that calls `self.skipWaiting()` on receipt of `SKIP_WAITING` is unreachable dead code. Because `self.skipWaiting()` is already called unconditionally in the `install` handler (line 17), the SW always activates immediately and is never in the waiting state when a client could send this message.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `self.skipWaiting()` unconditionally in install (line 17, pre-existing) ensures the SW transitions from installed to active without waiting. The message handler added by this PR at lines 30-34 calls `self.skipWaiting()` on a SW that is already active — a no-op. The dashboard.js code paths that send SKIP_WAITING (`if (reg.waiting)` and the statechange guard) are never triggered because `reg.waiting` stays null.
findings.severity_justification: Dead/redundant code causes no functional harm — the SW still activates correctly. The concern is misleading code that implies a coordination mechanism exists when it doesn't. Low severity on its own, though it points to the same design contradiction as Finding 1.
findings.category_justification: The handler is non-functional redundant code that misleads readers about the SW update flow — a maintainability/clarity issue rather than a runtime bug.

findings.message: The `reg.waiting` check (line 401) and the `updatefound` → `statechange` → `SKIP_WAITING` message flow (lines 405–416) are dead code. Because the SW calls `self.skipWaiting()` during `install`, it never enters the waiting state: `reg.waiting` is always null, and any newly found worker will have already self-activated before its `state` reaches `'installed'` in the waiting position.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `reg.waiting` is always null because `self.skipWaiting()` in install prevents the SW from ever entering the waiting state. The `updatefound`/`statechange` path technically executes but the SKIP_WAITING message it sends is a no-op since the SW already called `skipWaiting()` during install. Both code paths serve no functional purpose.
findings.severity_justification: Redundant/dead client-side code that adds complexity without benefit. No runtime bug on its own — the SW still activates correctly, just without user coordination as intended.
findings.category_justification: Code added by the PR that appears to implement a coordination mechanism but has no effect — misleads readers about how the update flow works.

findings.message: The fallback `return cached || networkFetch.catch(() => cached)` returns `undefined` when there is no cache entry (e.g. first visit) and the network request fails. `cached` is `undefined` in that case, so `networkFetch.catch(() => cached)` resolves to `undefined`. Passing a Promise that resolves to `undefined` to `event.respondWith()` causes the browser to synthesize a network error response rather than serving a useful fallback.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `caches.match()` resolves to `undefined` when no entry exists. `cached || networkFetch.catch(() => cached)` resolves to `undefined` when both are falsy. Passing a Promise resolving to `undefined` to `event.respondWith()` violates the spec and causes the browser to generate a network error rather than a useful fallback.
findings.severity_justification: Edge case requiring both no cached entry for a `/static/` asset AND network failure simultaneously. Pre-cached assets from ASSETS_TO_CACHE are largely protected, but any uncached static asset under network failure hits this bug.
findings.category_justification: Logic error where an invalid value (undefined) is returned to event.respondWith(), causing a network error instead of a graceful fallback.

findings.message: `event.waitUntil()` is called inside the async `.then()` callback of `caches.match()`, after the synchronous fetch event handler has already returned. The Service Worker spec requires `waitUntil()` to be invoked synchronously during event dispatch (before the dispatch flag is unset). While Chromium often tolerates this because `respondWith()` adds a pending promise that keeps the event active, it is a spec violation. In non-Chromium environments or in future spec-compliant runtimes, the background cache update may be silently abandoned before completion.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding incorrectly states that `waitUntil()` must be called synchronously during event dispatch. The SW spec only throws InvalidStateError when dispatch flag is unset AND timed-out flag is set — a conjunction. After sync dispatch, the timed-out flag is not set, so async `waitUntil()` is valid. This pattern is also the standard stale-while-revalidate approach used by Workbox and documented widely.
findings.severity_justification: Even if the concern were valid, the impact would be limited to background cache updates silently failing — not a user-visible error. Since the concern is factually wrong, severity is low.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns runtime reliability of the background cache update in various browser environments.

findings.message: The `updatefound` event can fire multiple times, but this code only adds a listener to the `reg.installing` worker that is present when `updatefound` first fires. If a new worker replaces the one currently installing before it reaches the 'installed' state, the 'statechange' listener will be on a stale worker object, and the `SKIP_WAITING` message will never be sent to the newest worker that eventually installs. This can leave the PWA in a state where an update is waiting but never activated.
findings.tp_fp_justification: `updatefound` fires for every new installing worker, not just once. Each firing captures `reg.installing` at that moment and attaches a `statechange` listener to that specific worker. If Worker A is superseded by Worker B, a second `updatefound` fires and attaches a listener to Worker B. The claim that SKIP_WAITING is never sent to the newest worker is incorrect.
findings.severity_justification: The finding describes a scenario that doesn't actually occur — each new worker gets its own listener through its own updatefound event.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about update coordination logic potentially failing to reach the newest worker, which would be a correctness issue if true.

findings.message: The service worker does not handle missing network responses when serving from the API (/api/). This could lead to unhandled errors or blank responses when the network is unavailable.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The API network-only behavior is intentional and documented in the code comment. When fetch() rejects, event.respondWith() synthesizes a network error identical to the pre-PR behavior of returning without calling respondWith(). No meaningful fallback exists for live NTP/GPS data. The finding is a generic 'no error handling' observation without a concrete actionable fix for this use case.
findings.severity_justification: Even if valid, behavior is the same as without a service worker — API calls fail when offline, which is expected for a real-time time/GPS dashboard.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about graceful degradation when the network is unavailable.

findings.message: When prompting a waiting service worker to activate using SKIP_WAITING, there is no synchronization to ensure that the message has actually been handled successfully. This can lead to a race condition where updates may not be fully applied before a page reload.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The `controllerchange` event IS the synchronization mechanism — it fires when the new SW calls clients.claim() after activation, confirming the new SW is fully in control before the page reloads. This is the standard recommended pattern for SW update coordination. The finding misidentifies existing synchronization as absent.
findings.severity_justification: The finding describes a non-existent race condition; the code correctly uses controllerchange as the synchronization point before reloading.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about a claimed race condition in the update coordination logic.

findings.message: The `updatefound` handler does not check for scenarios where the installing worker fails (e.g., due to corrupted cache files or resource loading errors), which could result in undefined behavior or missed updates.
findings.tp_fp_justification: When SW installation fails, state becomes 'redundant'. The existing `newWorker.state === 'installed'` check correctly excludes this — nothing is sent and the old SW continues normally. No undefined behavior occurs; the finding doesn't identify any concrete harmful outcome or specify what the error handler should do differently.
findings.severity_justification: Even if a check were added, the only actionable response would be a console log. No user-facing harm occurs when installation fails.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about not handling an error state in the SW installation flow.

findings.message: The CACHE_NAME versioning mechanism might cause unnecessary cache misses during updates if file URLs or cache keys remain unchanged. Consider more granular cache invalidation strategies.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is generic boilerplate about cache versioning strategy. It does not identify a concrete bug or harmful behavior — bumping CACHE_NAME is the standard, widely-used approach for service worker cache invalidation. 'Unnecessary cache misses' on update is the intended behavior: forcing fresh downloads of all assets on a new release. The suggestion to use 'more granular cache invalidation strategies' is vague advice applicable to any service worker codebase without referencing any specific issue in this one.
findings.severity_justification: Cache versioning causes full re-download on update, which is intentional and harmless in a small PWA with a handful of pre-cached assets.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about cache efficiency and unnecessary network requests from over-broad cache invalidation.

findings.message: The `newWorker.state === 'installed'` logic assumes a successful installation state but doesn't account for other potential states (e.g., 'redundant'). This could lead to sending SKIP_WAITING messages to invalid workers.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The condition `newWorker.state === 'installed'` is an exact equality check — it only sends SKIP_WAITING when the state is precisely 'installed'. If the worker transitions to 'redundant' or any other state, the condition is false and no message is sent. The finding claims this could send messages to invalid workers, but the strict equality check is exactly the mechanism that prevents that. Sending postMessage to a redundant worker is harmless anyway (no listener would act on it meaningfully). The finding contradicts the actual code logic.
findings.severity_justification: The strict equality check already handles all other states correctly by doing nothing. No harmful behavior is possible from this logic.
findings.category_justification: The finding makes a claim about incorrect state handling logic.

findings.message: This reloads on every `controllerchange`, including the first time the service worker takes control of a page. The updated worker calls `skipWaiting()` during install and `clients.claim()` during activation, so a first-time PWA visit can be forced through an immediate extra reload even though there is no update to apply. Gate the reload on an existing controller/update path so only real updates reload the page.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The diff explicitly captures `hadController = !!navigator.serviceWorker.controller` before registration and guards the reload with `if (isRefreshing || !hadController) { return; }`. This already prevents the reload on first install, which is exactly what the finding says is missing.
findings.severity_justification: An unguarded reload on first SW install would be a real UX issue, but the code already handles it correctly in the diff.
findings.category_justification: The claim is about incorrect runtime behavior — an unintended page reload on first install.

findings.message: The `SKIP_WAITING` message path starts an asynchronous `skipWaiting()` operation but does not attach it to the service worker event lifetime. Because this handler is part of the update handoff, use the message event's lifetime management so the worker cannot be stopped before the activation request completes and failures are not left as unhandled promises.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Factually correct: `self.skipWaiting()` is called but its returned Promise is not attached to the event lifetime via `event.waitUntil()`. The recommended pattern per SW spec is `event.waitUntil(self.skipWaiting())` to prevent the worker from being killed before activation completes. The finding names the specific handler and method.
findings.severity_justification: `skipWaiting()` is a fast internal operation that the spec guarantees always resolves, so the risk of the worker being killed mid-call is negligible in practice. The fix is trivial but the real-world impact of the missing `waitUntil` is minimal.
findings.category_justification: Concerns proper service worker event lifetime management — ensuring async operations complete before the worker can be terminated.
